opus-5.5.text:
Caching in agentic systems is a really interesting problem because it looks a lot like the memory hierarchy problems we've dealt with in computer architecture for decades, but with some new twists.

When you have an agent, you're not doing a single inference call. You're running a loop: the model reasons, calls a tool, gets a result, reasons again, maybe spawns sub-agents, and so on. Across all of those steps there's a huge amount of shared context: the system prompt, the tool definitions, the conversation history, documents that were retrieved. If you recompute the attention state for all of that on every step, you waste a lot of compute and add a lot of latency. So the first-order thing is that KV caching has to persist across agent steps, not just within a single generation.

That pushes you toward thinking about the KV cache as a first-class piece of state that needs to be managed, the way we manage data in a memory hierarchy. Some of it is hot and should sit in HBM next to the compute. Some of it is warm. You'll come back to it when the agent returns to a particular thread or a sub-task finishes, and that can live in a larger, cheaper tier like DDR. Some of it is cold and can be evicted or pushed further out. The systems that do well will have a big, fast memory tier behind the accelerator so they can hold a lot of these contexts and switch between them quickly, rather than recomputing prefill every time.

The second piece is reuse across agents and across users. In a multi-agent workflow you often have many agents sharing the same prefix: same instructions, same tools, same base documents. Prefix sharing and deduplication of that cached state can give you big savings, and the scheduler should be aware of it, so you route requests that share a prefix to wherever that state already lives. This is essentially locality-aware scheduling.

Third, I think caching extends beyond the KV cache. Agents call tools repeatedly: the same search, the same database query, the same code execution. Caching tool results, and even intermediate reasoning results, with appropriate invalidation, is another layer. Invalidation is the hard part, just like cache coherence is the hard part in multiprocessors. If the underlying data changes, you need to know which cached results are stale.

So my view is that agentic AI turns inference from a stateless, request-response problem into a stateful one. Caching has to be designed across the whole stack: the hardware memory hierarchy, the runtime that manages and moves the state, and the orchestration layer that understands the structure of the agent workflow. When those are co-designed, you get much better throughput and latency than treating each model call as an independent event.

r001.rationale: It describes an agent loop of reasoning, tool calls, and possible sub-agents, but not a pipeline where agents execute an LLM-generated plan.

r002.rationale: It proposes reusing shared prefixes and caching tool results, but does not propose caching agentic task plans for subsequent users.

r003.rationale: It calls for caching context and KV state across agent steps, as well as tool and intermediate reasoning results, which goes beyond caching only the final result.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. So caching in agentic systems is one of those problems where I think the hardware perspective actually matters a lot, because what you're really dealing with is a memory hierarchy problem, just at a very different granularity than we're used to.

Let me back up. In a traditional LLM serving stack, the dominant form of caching is the KV cache, the attention keys and values you've already computed for a prefix. And the whole game is prefix reuse. If two requests share a prompt prefix, you don't recompute it. That works beautifully for chat, where the system prompt is shared and the conversation is append-only.

Agents break that model in a few ways. First, the context is no longer append-only. An agent calls a tool, gets a result, maybe summarizes or discards part of its history, maybe branches into subagents. So the clean prefix structure gets fragmented. Second, the working set gets large. You've got tool outputs, retrieved documents, intermediate reasoning, and a lot of it is reused across many steps of the same task, but not necessarily as a contiguous prefix. And third, agents are long-running, so the temporal locality is spread out over seconds or minutes rather than milliseconds.

So what I'd argue for is thinking about it as a multi-level hierarchy, very much like we do with L1, L2, L3 and DRAM. At the lowest level you have the KV cache on the accelerator, and that's your scarce, expensive resource, so you want to be very deliberate about what lives there. Then you have host memory, then something like a distributed tier across nodes, and finally you have recomputation as your "miss" path. The interesting question is the policy. LRU is probably wrong for agents. You want policies that understand the structure of the computation, that a tool result is going to be referenced again at the next step, that a subagent's context is dead once it returns, that the system prompt and tool schemas are effectively pinned.

The other thing I'd push on is that caching shouldn't just be about attention state. Agents are enormously redundant at the semantic level. They call the same tools with the same arguments, they re-retrieve the same documents, they re-derive the same intermediate conclusions. So there's a layer of caching that's closer to memoization, caching tool results, caching retrieval results, maybe even caching plans or partial trajectories keyed by some canonicalized version of the task state. That's where you get the big wins, because you skip the entire forward pass, not just part of it.

And then from a systems point of view, the thing I care about is making the hardware and the scheduler aware of all of this. If you know a particular agent is going to come back in two seconds with a very similar context, you'd like to keep that state resident on the chip, or at least schedule it onto the same device, rather than scattering it around the cluster and paying the transfer cost. That's locality-aware scheduling, and it's the same intuition as cache affinity in a multicore, just applied to agent state.

So the short version is: treat it as a hierarchy, make the policies structure-aware rather than just recency-based, cache at the semantic level and not only the attention level, and co-design the scheduler with the cache so the state ends up where the compute is. I think the systems that get this right are going to be dramatically cheaper and faster than the ones that treat every agent step as an independent request.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents, tool calls, and cached plans, but does not describe a pipeline where an LLM-generated plan is executed by agents.

r002.rationale: It proposes caching plans or partial trajectories, but does not say they should be reused by subsequent users.

r003.rationale: It advocates caching semantic items such as tool and retrieval results, intermediate conclusions, plans, and partial trajectories, beyond attention state or final results.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to think about caching at several levels. There’s the caching inside the model itself—the KV cache, for example—but an agent also has context, tool results, and intermediate work that you may want to reuse. If every step starts from scratch, you’re spending a lot of computation rediscovering things you already know.

The interesting question is, when is that reuse valid? If you’ve cached a tool result and the underlying data has changed, you can send the agent down the wrong path. And two requests that sound similar may have different constraints, so similarity alone isn’t enough to decide that a cached answer is appropriate.

So I’d think of caching as part of the agent’s state management. You need to track what a result depends on, how fresh it is, and which user or task it belongs to. Then the system can reuse the portions of the computation that are still valid. That gives you an opportunity to reduce latency and cost while preserving correctness.

r001.rationale: It mentions agent steps and intermediate work, but does not describe a pipeline where an LLM-generated plan is executed by agents.

r002.rationale: It proposes reusing valid cached computation, but does not specifically propose caching task plans for reuse by subsequent users.

r003.rationale: It says agents may reuse context, tool results, and intermediate work, and that caching should track dependencies, freshness, and task ownership rather than only a final answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to think about caching at multiple levels. There’s the conventional caching of model state—the KV cache—but in an agentic system, you also want to reuse work across the steps of a task. If multiple agents are working with the same documents or the same context, you don’t want each one to process all of that from scratch.

Then there’s caching the results of tools and intermediate computations. The interesting question is, when is a previous result still valid? If it’s a calculation on fixed inputs, that’s relatively straightforward. If it’s information from a changing environment, you need some way to establish freshness and invalidate it.

So I’d like the system to make reuse efficient without making every agent developer manage all the details. But the application has to communicate enough about what can change and what can safely be shared. Otherwise, you can make the system faster while quietly making its answers less reliable.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reuse across task steps and agents, but does not describe a pipeline where agents execute an LLM-generated plan.

r002.rationale: It does not propose caching task plans for reuse by subsequent users.

r003.rationale: It describes caching model state, shared work, tool results, and intermediate computations, communicating reuse of task information beyond merely caching the final result.
